plain_english: A Roman man came in with his son to hear a lesson. Epictetus began teaching, then stopped. When the Roman asked him to continue, Epictetus said: This is how teaching works. Every skill causes struggle for someone who doesn't know it yet. But the things that come from these skills quickly show their purpose. Most skills have something attractive and pleasing about them. Watch someone learn to make shoes — it's not pleasant to see. But the finished shoe is useful and looks good. Watch a blacksmith learning his trade — it's painful to watch if you don't know the craft. But the final work shows the value of the skill. You'll see this most clearly with music. If you watch someone learning to play, it sounds terrible. But the results of music are beautiful and delightful, even to people who know nothing about music.
original_excerpt: When a certain Roman entered with his son and listened to one reading, Epictetus said, This is the method of instruction; and he stopped. When the Roman asked him to go on, Epictetus said, Every art when it is taught causes labor to him who is unacquainted with it and is unskilled in it, and indeed the things which proceed from the arts immediately show their use in the purpose for which they were made; and most of them contain something attractive and pleasing. For indeed to be present and to observe how a shoemaker learns is not a pleasant thing; but the shoe is useful and also not disagreeable to look at. And the discipline of a smith when he is learning is very disagreeable to one who chances to be present and is a stranger to the art: but the work shows the use of the art. But you will see this much more in music; for if you are present while a person is learning, the discipline will appear most disagreeable; and yet the results of music are pleasing and delightful to those who know nothing of music.

plain_english: Here's what we think a philosopher's job looks like: you must align your wishes with what's actually happening. That way, nothing that happens goes against what you want. And nothing that doesn't happen leaves you wishing it had. When you arrange your philosophy this way, you won't fail to get what you desire. You won't run into what you're trying to avoid. You'll live without anxiety, fear, or inner turmoil. And you'll maintain all your relationships properly — as a son, father, brother, citizen, human being, spouse, neighbor, fellow traveler, leader, or follower. This is what we think a philosopher's work looks like. The next question is: how do you actually do this?
original_excerpt: And here we conceive the work of a philosopher to be something of this kind: he must adapt his wish ([Greek: boulaesin]) to what is going on, so that neither any of the things which are taking place shall take place contrary to our wish, nor any of the things which do not take place shall not take place when we wish that they should. From this the result is to those who have so arranged the work of philosophy, not to fail in the desire, nor to fall in with that which they would avoid; without uneasiness, without fear, without perturbation to pass through life themselves, together with their associates maintaining the relations both natural and acquired, as the relation of son, of father, of brother, of citizen, of man, of wife, of neighbor, of fellow-traveller, of ruler, of ruled. The work of a philosopher we conceive to be something like this. It remains next to inquire how this must be accomplished.

plain_english: Look at how this works. A carpenter learns certain skills and becomes a carpenter. A ship pilot learns certain skills and becomes a pilot. So in philosophy, it's not enough to just want to be wise and good. You also need to learn certain things. What things? The philosophers say you should first learn that God exists and takes care of everything. You can't hide your actions from him. You can't even hide your intentions and thoughts. Next, you need to learn what the gods are like. Once you understand their nature, you must try with all your strength to be like them if you want to please and obey them. If the divine is faithful, you must be faithful. If it's free, you must be free. If it's generous, you must be generous. If it's noble, you must be noble. Since you're copying God, everything you do and say must match this fact.
original_excerpt: We see then that the carpenter ([Greek: techton]) when he has learned certain things becomes a carpenter; the pilot by learning certain things becomes a pilot. May it not then in philosophy also not be sufficient to wish to be wise and good, and that there is also a necessity to learn certain things? We inquire then what these things are. The philosophers say that we ought first to learn that there is a God and that he provides for all things; also that it is not possible to conceal from him our acts, or even our intentions and thoughts. The next thing is to learn what is the nature of the gods; for such as they are discovered to be, he, who would please and obey them, must try with all his power to be like them. If the divine is faithful, man also must be faithful; if it is free, man also must be free; if beneficent, man also must be beneficent; if magnanimous, man also must be magnanimous; as being then an imitator of God he must do and say everything consistently with this fact.
